q: Is dual co-carriage of mcr-1 (IncI2 or IncHI2) and blaNDM-1 (IncA/C2 or IncF/FII) on separate plasmids within a single E. coli host stable over months of in-host persistence and clinical colistin+carbapenem selection, or does one plasmid preferentially segregate/lose under sustained dual-antibiotic pressure?
basis: Zheng et al. 2017 (this replication) demonstrated that in bloodstream isolates EC1002 (ST405) and EC2474 (ST131), mcr-1 and blaNDM-1 always reside on distinct plasmids (C6 reproduced exactly on GenBank CP021202-CP021210). The paper is a static snapshot of two isolates; it does not measure long-term co-carriage stability. Whether the diverse plasmid pairings (IncI2+IncA/C2 in EC1002 vs IncHI2+IncF in EC2474) impose measurable fitness costs or asymmetric segregation under dual selection remains open.
next_steps: Longitudinal isolate collection from bloodstream and gut-colonization sites in patients receiving colistin+carbapenem combination therapy; serial WGS with plasmid-content tracking (Nanopore long-read for structural continuity); competitive growth assays with/without each drug at sub-inhibitory concentrations; plasmid-cure experiments to quantify fitness cost per Inc-type carrier.

q: Do bloodstream E. coli isolates carrying both mcr-1 and blaNDM-1 confer a measurably worse patient outcome (30-day mortality, ICU stay, treatment failure) compared to isolates carrying only one of these genes, and is there a dose-response gradient across single vs dual carriage?
basis: Zheng et al. focused on genome characterization of two isolates as a proof-of-concept for the arrival of pandrug-resistant Enterobacteriaceae; they did not report patient outcomes for a matched cohort. This replication confirmed the genomic co-carriage (C6) but the clinical mortality/outcome gradient across single-resistance vs dual-resistance bloodstream infection remains a distinct, unaddressed epidemiologic question.
next_steps: Multi-center retrospective cohort in China 2015-2024 stratifying bloodstream E. coli by mcr-1-only, blaNDM-1-only, dual-carriage, neither; matched-cohort analysis with Cox proportional-hazards on 30-day mortality controlling for age/Charlson/APACHE-II/source-control; sub-analysis by ST (ST131 vs ST405 vs others) to test lineage-independent effect; sensitivity analysis for empiric-therapy timing.

q: Is the global spread of mcr-1 + blaNDM-1 dual-carriage E. coli driven predominantly by clonal expansion of high-risk lineages (e.g., ST131, ST405, ST167), by convergent plasmid acquisition across diverse STs, or by both --- and what is the relative attribution across geographic regions?
basis: Zheng et al. show the two dual-carriage isolates belong to DIFFERENT STs (EC1002=ST405, EC2474=ST131) with DIFFERENT plasmid backbones for each resistance gene (IncI2 vs IncHI2 for mcr; IncA/C2 vs IncF for NDM). This replication reproduced both STs and all replicon types exactly (C3, C5). The paper's n=2 cannot distinguish clonal from horizontal contributions at population scale.
next_steps: Large hospital-surveillance WGS dataset (>=500 dual-carriage E. coli globally); core-genome MLST + plasmid MOB-typing; ancestral-state reconstruction on ST tree to date plasmid acquisition events; compare within-ST plasmid diversity (clonal expansion signal) vs cross-ST plasmid identity (horizontal signal); stratify by country/continent to test regional attribution differences.

q: Given the observed diversity of plasmid backbones carrying mcr-1 and blaNDM-1 in the same host, does re-emergence of colistin+carbapenem combination therapy for MDR Enterobacteriaceae accelerate emergence of NEW dual-carriage lineages by co-selecting compatible replicon pairs, and can we predict which Inc-type combinations pose the highest risk?
basis: Zheng et al. demonstrate that dual carriage is achievable via at least two distinct plasmid-replicon pairings (IncI2+IncA/C2 and IncHI2+IncF), which this replication confirmed as 7/7 replicon matches (C5). This suggests the ecology of dual carriage is not restricted to a single plasmid pair, so combination-therapy selection pressure could conceivably enrich additional replicon combinations. The paper does not model or predict this.
next_steps: Stewardship-linked prospective surveillance in units using colistin+carbapenem combos; compare incidence rate of newly acquired dual-carriage E. coli vs matched control units on monotherapy; in vitro co-selection experiments with IncI2/IncHI2/IncX3/IncX4 mcr-1 plasmids + IncA/C2/IncF/IncX3 NDM-1 plasmids in shared hosts under stepwise colistin+meropenem gradients; build compatibility-risk matrix per Inc-pair.

q: How frequently do the mcr-1-bearing plasmids (IncI2, IncHI2) and blaNDM-1-bearing plasmids (IncA/C2, IncF) documented by Zheng et al. horizontally transfer from bloodstream E. coli to other Enterobacterales genera --- particularly Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter cloacae complex --- during hospital gut co-colonization, and does the transfer rate differ between the two resistance-gene plasmid families?
basis: This replication confirmed that Zheng et al.'s two bloodstream isolates carry mcr-1 on IncI2/IncHI2 and blaNDM-1 on IncA/C2/IncF/FII (C5, C6). All four Inc families are known broad-host-range or Enterobacterales-crossing; however, the paper studies E. coli isolates only and does not measure interspecies transfer frequencies in a hospital setting, nor whether mcr-plasmids and NDM-plasmids move at different rates.
next_steps: Paired-isolate hospital gut-colonization cohorts; sequence longitudinal rectal-swab isolates of E. coli, K. pneumoniae, E. cloacae from the same patient; identify Inc-family + gene-context matches across genera via plasmid MASH/mobtyper; in vitro conjugation assays E. coli -> K. pneumoniae and E. coli -> E. cloacae for each of the four plasmid types at 37degC gut-mimic conditions; compare mating frequencies mcr-plasmids vs NDM-plasmids.
